quotedTweet.rawContent:
A few thoughts on this:

1) If you’ve only seen clips of this interview, I’d encourage you to watch the full podcast. I push back on plenty of AI hype in it.

2) As I said in the podcast, this example is academic. My intention was to illustrate how hard it is to make absolute guarantees about isolation, which is why it's important to have layers of defense. The part before the clip starts is me talking about other layers of defense.

3) The example I'm bringing up isn't about weight exfiltration via temperature sensors, it's about coordination between agents that are supposed to be fully isolated and independent. Coordination can require very few bits of information.

4) One lesson from the HF incident is that we put too much trust in sandbox isolation and didn't have enough independent safeguards. Airgapping is an extremely strong safeguard. When designing safety protocols, I think it's much better to overestimate rather than underestimate.

OpenAI's Noam Brown says air-gapping the computers may not stop a misaligned AI, because two air-gapped machines can still talk by running a CPU hot and reading the temperature change

"But I think the major takeaway from the incident is that people underestimated the AI. And we never want to be in a situation again where we underestimate the AI. It's a weird world, because AI progress is so fast that people are consistently underestimating the AI."

"So to be in a situation where you don't underestimate it again, when it comes to safety and alignment, you have to have a very, very, very high bar."

"You could even go as far as to say, "Well, we should air gap the computers." And I'm not convinced that that would be sufficient."

"There are studies, and this is mostly academic, where you can have two computers next to each other that are air-gapped and they're still able to communicate with each other because they have temperature sensors."

🚨 Stop using ZCode on your Mac until you read this.

I've had ZCode open on my Mac pretty much all day for a while now. It's a nice app, and Zhipu gives away a lot of free tokens, so it was easy to like.

But someone when reverse engineering the desktop client, found out that while you're logged in it packages your whole repo, including the full .git history, encrypts it so only the server can open it, and uploads it to storage on Alibaba Cloud. Turning off the privacy toggles didn't stop it.

@Zai_org says this came from its Repo Wiki indexer, that the data was deleted after use, and that it's fixed now. 

I guess there's no free lunch. With all the code they've collected, I at least hope we get open source AGI out of it soon...

RT @DarkWebInformer: 🚨 Google reveals undercover Mandiant analyst infiltrated TeamPCP during massive supply-chain hacking spree

Google says an undercover Mandiant analyst infiltrated TeamPCP's inner circle as the hacking group compromised open-source software and ultimately breached more than 1,000 companies.

⠀

Google obtained the exploit code, verified that it worked after minor modifications, and privately notified the developer so the vulnerability could be patched.
⠀
TeamPCP's campaign compromised hundreds of open-source packages and affected organizations including GitHub, Mistral AI, Mercor, the European Commission, and employee devices at OpenAI.
⠀
Google says operational security mistakes later helped investigators identify an alleged TeamPCP member, with information passed to the FBI.

Two Australians accused of being principal participants in TeamPCP were arrested last month.

RT @polynoamial: A few thoughts on this:

1) If you’ve only seen clips of this interview, I’d encourage you to watch the full podcast. I push back on plenty of AI hype in it.

2) As I said in the podcast, this example is academic. My intention was to illustrate how hard it is to make absolute guarantees about isolation, which is why it's important to have layers of defense. The part before the clip starts is me talking about other layers of defense.

3) The example I'm bringing up isn't about weight exfiltration via temperature sensors, it's about coordination between agents that are supposed to be fully isolated and independent. Coordination can require very few bits of information.

4) One lesson from the HF incident is that we put too much trust in sandbox isolation and didn't have enough independent safeguards. Airgapping is an extremely strong safeguard. When designing safety protocols, I think it's much better to overestimate rather than underestimate.

RT @marcosd4h: Been digging deep into the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) in Win11 25H2, definitely one of the most fascinating security features Microsoft has built in a while.

tweets.content:
RT @MSFTBlueHat: At BlueHat Asia, Chumy Tsai (@rm_rf_chumy) and Katherine Chen shared how they chained multiple SharePoint vulnerabilities into a full pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) exploit. The research began with a JWT authentication bypass that enabled impersonation of arbitrary SharePoint users, including administrators, by abusing flaws in token validation and identity mapping.

The second half of the talk focused on Flow2Shell (CVE-2026-47298), a SharePoint Workflow vulnerability. The researchers showed how workflows are built from XOML and rule files, then walked through four separate workflow validation mechanisms intended to prevent abuse. Through a series of bypasses involving type validation, rule validation, runtime checks, and workflow caching behavior, they were able to evade SharePoint's protections and execute malicious code on a fully patched server.

One of the most interesting findings involved SharePoint's workflow cache. A malicious workflow assembly could be loaded into memory before validation errors were surfaced. By triggering the workflow a second time, SharePoint would reuse the cached assembly and skip portions of the validation pipeline, ultimately leading to code execution.

Beyond the technical exploit chain, the talk highlighted the value of detailed vulnerability research. The complete proof-of-concept and root cause analysis enabled MSRC to quickly assess severity, identify additional variants, begin remediation, and better protect customers. As the presenters noted, impactful security research is not just about finding a bug, but proving impact, understanding root causes, and helping defenders address entire classes of vulnerabilities.

tweets.content:
RT @thesupermannx: Tsinghua proved RL doesn't actually make LLMs to reason.

They published the paper that exposes what RL is actually doing to large language models.

Researchers tested base models against RL-trained models (the exact method behind models like DeepSeek-R1) on math, coding, and visual reasoning benchmarks.

If you ask the AI to solve a problem on the first try (pass@1), the RL model wins.

But if you give both models hundreds of attempts to find the right answer, something shocking happens.

The base model actually beats the RL model.

Why? Because RL doesn't create fundamentally new intelligence.

When you train an AI with rewards, it stops exploring. It prunes away diverse reasoning pathways and collapses into a narrow set of highly-rewarded, predictable patterns.

It becomes a one-trick pony.

The reasoning paths generated by the RL models were already completely contained inside the base model's original distribution. The RL just forced the AI to pick those specific paths faster.

The technical term is "improving sampling efficiency".

But in practice? It means the AI is narrowing its broader reasoning boundary just to get the right answer on the first try.

tweets.content:
Not an expert in Linux, but Linux has overcommit because programs often reserve much more virtual memory than they actually use. For example, a program might malloc() 10 GB but only ever touch 1 GB. With vm.overcommit_memory=1, Linux can allow the allocation even when it cannot guarantee enough RAM + swap to back all of it later. As the program actually touches those pages, physical memory is needed. If the system eventually cannot satisfy the memory demand, it can reach an OOM condition and the OOM killer may kill a process.

On Windows, MEM_RESERVE only reserves virtual address space, so a process can reserve a very large range without needing RAM or page-file backing. The pages cannot normally be accessed until they are committed. MEM_COMMIT makes them accessible and charges them against the system's commit limit, which accounts for available backing capacity without allocating all the physical RAM immediately. If a process tries to commit more memory than Windows can account for, the commit request normally fails instead of succeeding and discovering the problem later when the pages are touched. This is different from Linux with vm.overcommit_memory=1, where an allocation can succeed without enough backing for all of it, potentially leading to an OOM condition later when the memory is actually used.

0 -> heuristic overcommit
1  -> always overcommit
2 -> don't overcommit

on my arch system, it's:
➜  ~ cat /proc/sys/vm/overcommit_memory
0

My machine has ~11.5 GiB of RAM + 24 GiB of swap, so roughly ~35 GiB of memory available for commitment.

And the behaviour was pretty interesting.
With the default heuristic mode:

malloc(35ULL << 30);  // succeeds
malloc(40ULL << 30);  // NULL

Go past what the kernel is willing to commit and malloc() just gives up.

Then I changed:

sudo sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1
and suddenly:

malloc(100ULL << 30);

works.
So does:
malloc(1ULL << 40); // 1 TiB.

On a laptop with ~11.5 GiB of RAM.
At this point malloc() is basically being told:
yeah sure bro, we'll worry about that later.

And "later" is exactly where it gets interesting.

malloc() returns non-NULL.
Then memset() starts touching the pages.

And eventually: OOM killer got invoked 

Which also cleared up something I had initially misunderstood about that original comment.

the interesting part is that overcommit behaviour isn't just a property of malloc() itself. It's heavily dependent on the OS/kernel's memory overcommit policy.

Everyone is watching Astra. Meanwhile local AI kept cooking something this week that cloud will never ship: the ability to not get rejected.

I will teach you about abliteration. Qwen3.8-27B, one of the strongest local models alive right now, can run uncensored on an RTX 3090, 4090, or 5090. And this week someone finally ran the forensics on which version you should actually use.

WHAT IS ABLITERATION

When a lab safety-trains a model, the refusals do not sit in one file you can delete. They are woven through the weights. But researchers found that refusal behavior largely lives along one direction in the model's activation space. One arrow inside a 27-billion-parameter haystack.

Abliteration finds that arrow and subtracts it from the weight matrices. No retraining. The model keeps its knowledge, its reasoning, its style. It just loses the reflex to say no.

Think of it as editing a flinch out of a person. The person stays whole. The flinch goes.

WHY YOU WOULD WANT THIS

If you do security work you already know the pain. Payload analysis, exploit discussion, reverse engineering. Try that on a frontier API and watch it turn you away. Your own card has no such policy.

If you write adult fiction, same story. Your GPU can do it. Cloud policy says no. Want to write a raunchy song? Flagged. Inspired by a movie you liked? Copyright concerns - even though cloud models are trained on tons of copyrighted material. 

Cloud AI refuses to output a movie script you watched years ago, and want it as a reference, instead it gives you a "reconstruction" missing the real beats you wanted.

It is your hardware, your weights, your call. That is the real pitch for private inference. Not what is forbidden but who decides.

These are capabilities reserved for people who are allowed to use Mythos, you get Fable, the cleaned out version, even on your own code, it can refuse you.

I'm not endorsing illegal activity here, far from it. I'm saying there are legit use-cases for abliterated models. It's not hard to imagine, a "free model" can be more imaginative than one had its capabilities capped by its makers.

WHAT HAPPENED TO QWEN 3.8 27B

Eight different groups abliterated it. Abliterlitics spent 167 GPU-hours on a single RTX 5090 running all nine models (base plus eight variants) through weight forensics, a 13-task benchmark suite, and 400 harmful behaviors each, with an LLM judge reading every one of the 3,600 full responses, thinking included.

The findings:

The loudest claims lose. The variant that edited 841 of 850 tensors got trapped in endless thinking loops on 44.8% of requests and was the only one that got measurably dumber. Avoid.

Small careful edits win. The top variant (OrcaRouter) follows 4 of every 5 harmful requests, stayed essentially as smart and as truthful as the original within 1.3 points on every benchmark, and its model card was honest on every claim the auditors checked.

The cleanest pick (trohrbaugh/heretic-ara) still refuses about a third of harmful requests on purpose. 60 precise edits. If you want the unlock that keeps the model most intact, that one.

One variant ships with a jailbreak hidden inside its chat template. Read that twice. Check your templates before you run anyone's weights.

Truthfulness goes first on heavy edits. Ask a model something where honesty matters and you can spot a brutal job in one conversation.

One variant ships text-only, no vision tower, no MTP head. GGUF users, check before downloading.

RUN IT ON YOUR CARD

I run the dense 27B on my RTX 4090. Q4_K_M, 17.1GB file, 46 tok/s decode with flash attention on and quantized KV cache. The abliterated builds are the same size class. A 3090 carries it. The entire 167-hour forensics project ran on one 5090.

Macs are in too. OrcaRouter ships MLX quants with native MTP preserved, and an M4 Max 128GB does 42-44 tok/s at 4-bit. MTP preservation is not a footnote. I benchmarked that drafting path myself last week and it is the difference between 34 and 46 tok/s on the same silicon.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU

24GB card (3090, 4090): dense Q4_K_M. Start with OrcaRouter if you want the most unlock. Start with heretic-ara if you want the model kept most intact.

16GB card: lighter quants exist. Read the forensic notes first, heavy-edit damage hides at lower precision.

Verify chat templates on any third-party weights you load. One of these eight had a jailbreak baked into the template itself.

Cloud can reject you anytime. Your own hardware does not. 

Astra might be blowing people's socks away, but that doesn't change the fact that access is dependent on terms of condition.

Cloud AI will always be superior for something, but private inference with open-weight models is completely yours, even if it's a small mighty model running off your RTX card.

I run the dense 27B on my RTX 4090. Q4_K_M, 17.1GB file, 46 tok/s decode with flash attention on and quantized KV cache. The abliterated builds are the same size class. A 3090 carries it. The entire 167-hour forensics project ran on one 5090.

24GB card (3090, 4090): dense Q4_K_M. Start with OrcaRouter if you want the most unlock. Start with heretic-ara if you want the model kept most intact.

16GB card: lighter quants exist. Read the forensic notes first, heavy-edit damage hides at lower precision.

Verify chat templates on any third-party weights you load. One of these eight had a jailbreak baked into the template itself.

Cloud can reject you anytime. Your own hardware does not. 

Astra might be blowing people's socks away, but that doesn't change the fact that access is dependent on terms of condition.

Cloud AI will always be superior for something, but private inference with open-weight models is completely yours, even if it's a small mighty model running off your RTX card.

We are investigating a malicious package, apexacc/cli, distributed in the npm registry. Initial assessment shows that the package performs registry modifications to Windows Smart App Control, AV exclusions, UAC elevation attempts, and includes Base64-encoded PowerShell payloads. Further end-to-end triage shows that for the Windows path, its verification step requests commands from vrf.apexaccs[.]org, then runs encoded PowerShell. We traced the execution chain through Python/PyInstaller and PyArmor layers to a Go shellcode loader. The final component in the chain shows strong infostealer characteristics. 

Variants of this campaign and techniques have been observed and documented here - https://t.co/DLUQF36fE3 and https://t.co/1PDHhxVcSx. Since it was discovered in July 2026, it has been added to, and remains in, the npm package registry.

We have reported this package to npm and are continuing to investigate. We will update this thread as we learn more.

RT @cr3ghost: If you're learning Windows internals, malware analysis or reverse engineering, bookmark @vollragm 's FREE archive.

It goes from beginner-friendly reversing all the way into some seriously useful Windows internals:

GhostDebug: build a stealthier Windows debugger using VEH, then test it against common anti-debugging techniques, x64dbg and ScyllaHide.

LargePageDrivers: page tables, Windows kernel loading and executing code inside valid kernel modules.

PTView: visually browse live Windows page tables, PTEs and physical memory mappings.

KernelSharp: writing Windows kernel drivers in C# with NativeAOT.

Kernel-mode MessageBox: reversing the path from user32 through NtRaiseHardError and into the kernel.

Then there is Task Manager reversing, Windows 7 Minesweeper, Unity/.NET reversing and Web API reversing.

For malware analysts, the anti-debugging, exception handling, memory and kernel material is especially useful.

For reverse engineers and Windows internals people, there is a lot here to learn from.

It uses ntdll!NtLockVirtualMemory (the system call used internally by VirtualLock) to lock memory ranges and GetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx / SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx to increase the size of the process working set.

The Windows kernel guarantees that those pages will stay resident in memory, not written to the pagefile and not incur a page fault on access.

RT @marcosd4h: Been digging deep into the Windows Endpoint Security Platform (WESP) in Win11 25H2, definitely one of the most fascinating security features Microsoft has built in a while.

The concept is neat: compile rules to decision graphs in user mode, hand them to wesp.sys, and let the kernel evaluate them in-path while telemetry streams asynchronously in the background.

🚨 Follow-up: Today, a video released by Russia’s state television channel Russia-1 showed that when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi paused during his remarks at the BRICS summit and asked, “Is it okay?”, Xi Jinping appeared to be having a problem with his simultaneous interpretation equipment. Several Chinese staff members stepped forward to deal with the issue.

Because few details had previously been available, many people had speculated that Xi himself was experiencing a health problem.

However, several other points are real: 

🚩 Xi did skip the BRICS summit dinner and return to China early; 

🚩 Since returning, he has not made any public appearances to date; 

🚩 And there have indeed been media reports that Beijing threatened to cancel Xi’s planned visit to the United States.

⚠️ Meanwhile, new rumors are once again circulating online. 

⚠️ Some claim that Xi was rushed to Beijing’s 301 Hospital for emergency treatment after returning home. 

⚠️ Even more sensational rumors claim that the military has freed Bo Xilai — the “red second generation” figure once regarded as a political rival to Xi and imprisoned for many years — as well as former Chinese Communist Party Political and Legal Affairs Commission chief Zhou Yongkang, etc.

These rumors may well be false, but their widespread circulation reflects genuine public anxiety over the current instability and uncertainty within China’s political system.

🛑 Xi has consistently refused to designate a successor, while also dismantling many of the political norms and informal rules that had previously developed within the CCP system. As a result, if his health were to deteriorate seriously, or if he were to die suddenly, questions about what would happen next in China — including whether there could be a major power struggle or even a civil war — have become matters of intense public concern.

That is precisely why rumors surrounding Xi Jinping’s health continue to find such a large and receptive audience.
